article.headline: SK Hynix's Frankfurt GDR Fell 15%—Its Seoul Shares Rose 3%
article.lede: On the morning of May 7, 2026, SK hynix's Frankfurt-listed depositary receipt fell roughly 15% in thirty minutes while Micron, DRAM futures, and the iShares MSCI South Korea ETF sat unmoved. The divergence looked alarming. It wasn't: the underlying Seoul-listed shares rose 3% that same session, and the answer to "why" lies entirely in the mechanics of a thinly traded secondary instrument cut off from its home exchange.
article.body:
The instrument in question, trading in Frankfurt under the GDR ticker HY9H, represents ordinary shares of SK hynix (000660.KS) held in custody in Seoul by a depositary bank. *Global Depositary Receipts* exist to give European institutional investors exposure to foreign-listed companies without requiring them to navigate Korean settlement infrastructure, *won* currency conversion, or local foreign-investor registration requirements. Each receipt represents a fractional or whole claim on underlying Korea Exchange (KRX) shares; in theory, the GDR price should track the underlying in real time, adjusted for the conversion ratio and the KRW/EUR exchange rate.

In practice, that parity depends on live arbitrage—and live arbitrage requires a functioning two-way market. Frankfurt's GDR market for SK hynix (000660.KS) is a specialist venue: a designated market maker maintains quotes but faces no obligation to absorb large blocks at fair value. More critically, the KRX closes at 3:30 PM Seoul time, translating to roughly 8:30 AM in Frankfurt. Any trade after that point proceeds without a live price anchor on the home exchange. Reconstructing the cross-border arbitrage—buying KRX shares in Seoul, depositing them with a custodian, issuing new GDR units, and selling them in Frankfurt—takes days, not seconds. A single institutional seller with no willing counterpart can drive the Frankfurt quote down 15% before the price-equalizing mechanism has any chance to engage.

The absence of a fundamental driver is confirmed by the Seoul data. 000660 closed at ₩1,654,000 on May 7, **up 3.31%** from the prior session. Micron (MU) was flat, DRAM forward prices were flat, and EWY—which holds KRX-listed 000660 shares and prices them from Seoul—reflected that positive session accordingly. The 15% Frankfurt print carried no fundamental signal. It was a thin-book dislocation on a secondary venue, the kind of artifact that sophisticated traders sometimes exploit as an arbitrage entry rather than interpret as a market view.

The disconnect is sharpest precisely because SK hynix's (000660.KS) underlying story in May 2026 is one of exceptional momentum. The company reported Q1 2026 revenues of ₩52.6 trillion—up 198% year-on-year—with a 72% operating margin driven almost entirely by *high-bandwidth memory* (HBM), the densely stacked DRAM chips that sit between GPU and processor in every major AI accelerator. SK hynix holds more than half of the global HBM market and supplies roughly two-thirds of demand from Nvidia (NVDA) for HBM4, the latest variant slated for Nvidia's Vera Rubin AI platform. Any genuine bad news would move the KRX price first. On May 7, there was none.

concepts.definition: A security issued by a depositary bank that represents shares in a foreign company held in custody on the home exchange. Investors buy the GDR instead of the underlying share to avoid navigating foreign settlement systems, currency accounts, or local registration rules. In theory the GDR tracks the underlying price; in practice, thin liquidity and cross-border settlement latency can produce large temporary divergences from fair value.

A form of DRAM in which multiple memory dies are stacked vertically and connected by microscopic through-silicon vias, dramatically increasing data throughput compared with conventional modules. HBM sits directly beside the GPU die on a shared substrate, providing the bandwidth that large AI model inference and training demand. SK hynix pioneered commercial HBM production and retains the leading market share, ahead of Samsung and Micron.

Dynamic Random-Access Memory—the dominant form of volatile working memory in computers, servers, and AI accelerators. Data in DRAM must be constantly refreshed and is lost when power is cut, but access speeds are far faster than storage-class memory. Three companies—SK hynix, Samsung, and Micron—control roughly 95% of global DRAM supply.

South Korea's principal securities exchange, which operates the Korea Stock Exchange for equities and closes each trading day at 3:30 PM Seoul time. Because that translates to roughly 8:30 AM Central European Time, GDRs of Korean companies traded in Frankfurt enter an hours-long window each session where there is no live home-market price anchor, leaving them vulnerable to microstructure dislocations.

In Frankfurt's model for low-volume securities, a designated specialist both quotes prices and executes trades. The specialist must maintain two-sided quotes but may widen bid-ask spreads aggressively when order flow is thin or one-sided. Unlike a deep electronic order book with many competing participants, a specialist model provides limited price support when a large sell order arrives with no natural counterpart.

Nvidia's next-generation AI accelerator platform, succeeding the Blackwell architecture. Vera Rubin integrates HBM4 memory and targets large-scale AI training and inference workloads in data centers. SK hynix has been confirmed as the primary HBM4 memory supplier for the platform, expected to begin mass production in 2026.

ticker_000660-ks.name: SK hynix Inc.
ticker_000660-ks.blurb: SK hynix Inc. researches, develops, manufactures, and sells semiconductor devices, including DRAM, NAND flash, SSD, MCP, and CMM products. The company serves server, networking, mobile, PC, consumer, and automotive markets. It is one of the world's largest memory chipmakers, competing directly with Samsung Electronics and Micron Technology.
ticker_000660-ks.recent: In the past 30 days, SK hynix reported earnings on April 23, 2026, with revenue and net income surging on a memory price upcycle. The stock hit a 52-week high of 1,653,000 KRW, reflecting strong demand for AI-related memory chips. Morningstar raised its fair value estimate by 65% following the earnings report.

ticker_mu.name: Micron Technology, Inc.
ticker_mu.blurb: Micron is the only US-headquartered manufacturer of DRAM and NAND memory at scale, competing with Samsung and SK Hynix. Historically the most cyclical of the three, it has spent the past two years repositioning toward high-bandwidth memory (HBM), the stacked DRAM that pairs with AI accelerators, where pricing is multiples of standard DDR5 and contracts are multi-year rather than spot.
ticker_mu.recent: In March 2026 Micron began mass production of HBM4 12-Hi 36GB stacks for Nvidia's Vera Rubin platform; management has stated 2026 HBM capacity is sold out under binding agreements. Fiscal Q2 2026 revenue was around $23.9 billion, with non-GAAP gross margin near 75%. The board approved a 30% dividend increase and roughly $25 billion of fiscal-2026 capex. Despite a strong year-to-date move, the forward P/E remains in the high single digits on consensus, reflecting residual cyclicality scepticism.

ticker_nvda.name: NVIDIA Corporation
ticker_nvda.blurb: NVIDIA designs graphics processing units (GPUs) and system-on-chip products. Originally a gaming chip company, it became the dominant supplier of AI accelerators — chips that perform the parallel matrix math required to train and run large language models. Its H100, H200, and Blackwell GPU families are the de facto standard for AI training infrastructure at hyperscalers and cloud providers. NVIDIA's CUDA software ecosystem creates deep switching costs: virtually all AI frameworks and models are optimised for CUDA, making competing hardware difficult to adopt at scale. NVIDIA also sells networking (InfiniBand, Ethernet) and data-centre systems.
ticker_nvda.recent: NVIDIA reported FY2026 (ending Jan 2026) revenue of $215.9 billion, up 65% YoY, with data centre revenue reaching $186 billion. The company's forward P/E of ~17.5x on 34.8% projected EPS growth produces a PEG of 0.50 — unusually cheap for what is arguably the most critical infrastructure company in the AI buildout. Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta) collectively committed over $200 billion in AI infrastructure capex for 2026, the majority flowing through NVIDIA's supply chain.
